title: From strength to strength (Berakhot 64a, Psalm 84:8)
hook: scholars have no rest; they "go from strength to strength"
tomorrow: a whole book of blessings is about to end. on what word?

segments.voice: Yesterday Hillel's rule: step back where the crowd is, step in where nobody is. Fill the gap. And once it's filled, can you stop?
screen: `FILL THE GAP.` → `AND THEN, CAN YOU STOP?`

segments.voice: Finish the semester, then rest. Finish the project, then rest. Retire, then rest. A lot of life runs on a finish line just ahead. So, when do the wise finally get to rest? The Talmud's answer, near the very end of Berakhot, sounds at first like bad news. Never. Not in this world, and not in the next one either. Then it quotes a psalm, and the bad news turns out to be something else.
screen: `FINISH, THEN REST.` → `WHEN DO THE WISE REST?` → `NEVER. THEN A PSALM.`

segments.voice: The question: is there a finish line? Rabbi Hiyya bar Ashi, in the name of Rav, says those who learn Torah have no rest, in this world or the world to come. The proof is Psalm 84: "They go from strength to strength, every one of them appeareth before God in Zion." In Hebrew, mechayil el chayil. Read it again. No rest doesn't mean no relief, worn out forever. It means no standing still. Each strength becomes the ground for the next one. That's the answer here: the reward for growing is more growing. Now a neighbor. Owen's tradition, Christianity, has a line that sounds close. Paul writes to the church at Philippi, in the King James Bible: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark." Shared ground: neither text lets you coast on what you've already done. Both keep a person moving forward, toward God. And an honest difference. Paul's next words name a prize at the end of the race, "the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus." Christians read their goal through Jesus. The sages describe no last lap at all: even in the world to come, the learning goes on, strength after strength. Here's something to tell a friend tonight: a Jewish custom: when a book of the Torah is finished aloud, the congregation calls out chazak, chazak, venitchazek: be strong, be strong, and we'll be strengthened. Finishing is where the next strength starts.
screen: `IS THERE A FINISH LINE?` · `NO STANDING STILL.` · `A NEIGHBOR: I PRESS TOWARD THE MARK.` · `A PRIZE, OR NO LAST LAP.` · then, large: `FROM STRENGTH TO STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Stand up and walk slowly for one minute, in a room or a hallway. With each few steps, name one thing you've finished lately. Then stop, and name the next small step it makes possible.
screen: `WALK SLOWLY.` · `NAME WHAT YOU FINISHED.` · `NAME THE NEXT STEP.`

segments.voice: From strength to strength. The psalm the Talmud uses for people who learn: no standing still, each strength the ground for the next.
Your line: from strength to strength, no last lap. Forty-five of fifty, and still going.

screen: `DAY 1532 COUNTS.` → `BERAKHOT · 45 OF 50.` → `TOMORROW: A WHOLE BOOK OF BLESSINGS IS ABOUT TO END. ON WHAT WORD?`

howItsDone: When a book of the Torah is finished in the synagogue reading, the congregation calls out chazak, chazak, venitchazek; the phrase from strength to strength is also a common Jewish wish for someone's next step.
